newsitem.title: GREECE: EU plans to boost renewable energy sources by 2010.
newsitem.headline: EU plans to boost renewable energy sources by 2010.

text.p: The EU Commissioner for Energy, Christos Papoutsis, disclosed on Monday plans for installing half a million solar power units in Europe by the year 2010.

Speaking at a three-day conference on renewable energy sources in Athens, Papoutsis announced he would adopt a strategy aimed at doubling the contribution of renewable sources of energy to total energy needs in the European Union to 12 percent by year 2010.
He also said he favoured the construction of a solar power station in Crete, Greece's southernmost island, a plan he had put forward in 1995.
The Greek division of Greenpeace endorsed Papoutsis' plans.
"Greenpeace took a positive view on the EU Commissioner's plans," said Elias Efthymiopoulos, director of Greenpeace's Greek division.

"Without substantial use of solar power and other renewable energy sources it is impossible to attain the EU's targets for a 15 percent cut in carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2010," Greenpeace said.
Greenpeace says Greece may step up the use of solar power from current very low levels.
"A 30 percent portion of Greece's total energy needs may be met by roof-top solar power units, according to an EU study," said Stelios Psomas, Greenpeace's energy official.
Greenpeace has put forward a plan for installing solar power units in houses, schools, public buildings and factories.
Europe is lagging behind the US and Japan with respect to solar power technology, it said.
US vice-president Al Gore recently announced a programme aimed at providing solar power capacity to one million buildings in the US over a 10-year period.
Japan is already financing a programme for 70,000 solar power roof-tops units, targeting an aggregate solar power capacity of 400 MW by the year 2000 and 4,600 MW by 2010, Greenpeace said.
It cited EU studies suggesting that widespread use of solar power units would create over 294,000 new jobs in the EU by year 2010.
The global market for solar power units is estimated at $1.13 billion and is growing at an annual rate of 15 percent, it said.

Solar power units are capable of converting between five and 15 percent of solar energy into electricity. They have a very long projected life, up to 30 years, and require minimal maintenance. Their operation does not produce noise or pollutants.
